mamma-roma-1962.gazette: Pasolini built the film out of the borgate themselves — the postwar blocks thrown up on Rome's outer edge — and filled the frame with people who lived there rather than actors who could imitate them. The method came straight from the neorealist decade before it: real streets, real faces, a subproletariat Italian cinema had only recently learned to look at directly. What the camera records is a place, not a set dressed to resemble one.

black-girl-1966.gazette: Sembène shot on both ends of the crossing, Dakar and Antibes, in real apartments and real streets, and cast a lead with no acting career behind her. The subject is domestic service: a Senegalese woman brought to the Riviera to work in a white family's flat, six years after independence. African cinema had almost no feature-length precedent to lean on, and this one arrived with its realism already staked.

mouchette-1967.gazette: Bresson did not call them actors. He called them models, cast them without professional experience, and drilled the expression out of their line readings until what remained was flat and exact. Music enters the film barely at all; the realism here is enforced by subtraction, inside the same social-realist lineage the neorealists opened.
mouchette-1967.prism: Strip the performance out and nothing stands between the viewer and the event — no actor's grief absorbing it on your behalf. That's the cost of the method: by the end there is no performance left to hide behind.

the-cow-1969.gazette: Mehrjui took the production into a real village and shot rural life at its own speed — subsistence, superstition, a man's whole livelihood standing in a single animal. The film is generally marked as the start of the Iranian New Wave, and its argument was made in method before theme: the village as location, not backdrop. Very little of the poverty on screen had to be constructed.

kes-1970.gazette: The cast came out of Barnsley — a local schoolboy in the lead, the rest drawn from the same coalfield — and Loach shot in the actual schools and streets. The Yorkshire speech was left uncorrected, thick enough that distributors abroad worried audiences would not follow it. The documentary habits show in the shooting itself: long lenses, real classrooms, a boy and a kestrel.

stroszek-1977.gazette: Herzog wrote the part for Bruno S. and then largely let him be himself in it, a Berlin street musician playing a Berlin street musician. The American stretch was filmed in rural Wisconsin with locals appearing as versions of themselves, in their own auction yards and bars, much of it unscripted. The result sits closer to documentation than to performance.
stroszek-1977.prism: Casting someone as a near-version of himself buys authenticity no director can manufacture, and it puts a real life on screen without the cover a character provides. Bruno S. carries the film and pays for it in the same frames.

where-is-the-friend-s-house-1987.gazette: The lead is a child with no training, and Kiarostami simply lets him walk — up the zigzag hill, back down, across the village, in takes that refuse to shorten the distance. Tedium is part of the contract: an errand this small only registers if the film gives it real time. Iranian neorealism starts less from subject matter than from that patience.

salaam-bombay-1988.gazette: Nair recruited children already living on Bombay's streets, ran them through a workshop before shooting began, and then filmed in the districts they came from. The camera works out in the actual traffic of the markets, pavements and red-light lanes, at documentary distance. The verité was not a style applied later; it was settled at casting.

the-story-of-qiu-ju-1992.gazette: Zhang hid cameras in the streets and markets of rural Shaanxi and let scenes play out among people who did not know a film was running. Non-professionals fill most of the roles, and the locations are the ones the story concerns — village, township office, county court. The bureaucratic runaround has the texture of the real thing because nearly everything around it is.
the-story-of-qiu-ju-1992.prism: Hidden cameras buy an authenticity that consent would have spoiled; the passersby read as real precisely because nobody asked them. Part of the film's realism is borrowed from people who never agreed to lend it.

the-fugitive-1993.gazette: The production worked in Chicago itself, filming the St. Patrick's Day parade during the actual parade and closing streets around a script still being rewritten between setups. The train wreck was staged practically, on real track, and the crew shot what happened. Much of what reads as documentary is a screenplay that had not yet caught up with its locations.

la-promesse-1996.gazette: The Dardennes came out of documentary and kept the habits: handheld camera, faces without screen history, and Seraing — their own post-industrial town — standing for itself. Undocumented labour and a father's small business are filmed where such arrangements actually occur, at working distance. No shot in the film asks to be read as anything but Belgium.

children-of-heaven-1997.gazette: Majidi filmed in the alleys of south Tehran, narrow enough that the camera has to run alongside the children rather than watch from somewhere comfortable. The plot turns on one lost pair of shoes, poverty measured in an object instead of a speech. The realism lives in the scale of the stake.
children-of-heaven-1997.prism: A film about child poverty that never raises its voice loads everything onto the object: one pair of shoes has to carry what an argument would. It works, and it also lets an audience leave feeling warm about something that isn't.

taste-of-cherry-1997.gazette: Kiarostami cast non-professionals and then kept them apart — the two men talking in the car were often filmed separately, each addressing the director sitting off-camera in the other seat. The conversations still hold, which is the method's claim: the realism is assembled shot by shot rather than performed. The dust roads in the hills outside Tehran do the rest.

central-station-1998.gazette: Salles found his young lead shining shoes at a Rio airport and put him opposite one of Brazil's most experienced actresses, then shot in the station the film is named for and on the roads running north from it. The crowds in frame are crowds, not extras arranged to resemble them. Brazilian street life supplies the material, not the décor.

not-one-less-1999.gazette: The villagers play themselves here — a schoolgirl standing in as the substitute teacher, pupils as pupils, shopkeepers behind their own counters — and the school is the kind of underfunded rural classroom the story is about. None of the principal cast had acted before. The docu-fiction mode carries the argument: the room is not a reconstruction.
not-one-less-1999.prism: When people play themselves, the film gets to enter their lives as evidence, and the shortage it documents becomes a story told in a register the authorities can live with. Both of those things are true of the same footage.
